name: Sandy Lane
label: Sandy Lane
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sandy Lane Beach' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Famous luxury resort and beach south of Holetown.

text.description:
Sandy Lane is a five-star beachfront resort close to Holetown and Paynes Bay. Ronald Tree, a former British politician, opened it in 1961 as a luxury hotel and golf course on what had been a sugar plantation. The original resort was pulled down after a group of Irish businessmen bought it in 1998, and it was rebuilt over about three years. Today it has 113 guestrooms and suites, a five-bedroom villa, four restaurants, seven bars and three golf courses. Tiger Woods married here in 2004.

For a phone photo, the best scene is not the hotel building but the beach along the resort frontage. The hotel's pink loungers and parasols make a bright foreground against pale sand and calm turquoise water, and the shoreline gives you a natural line running across the frame. Stand on the public sand, about 412 m south of the hotel, rather than in the hotel's lounger area, which belongs to the hotel. Keep the horizon level using your gridlines, and let the loungers fill the lower third of the picture. Tap on the water or the loungers to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sand looks washed out. The beach can be busy, so an early visit may give you fewer people in the frame.
text.geographic_location: Sandy Lane is a beachfront resort close to Holetown and Paynes Bay.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops serve this spot. Head to Sandy Lane Beach, then follow the pathway to the right of the One Sandy Lane development down to the public sand. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the loungers and parasols with sea behind them. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in more of the beach and water, keeping the horizon level so it does not bend at the edges. If your phone has a telephoto lens (2x-5x), use it to pick out a neat row of parasols.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows the hotel's pink loungers and parasols along the resort frontage, with white sand and calm turquoise water stretching along the frame. The hotel itself lies to the north. Stay on the public sand and out of the hotel's lounger area.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line, so the loungers and sand fill the lower two-thirds. Crouch a little to bring the parasols up against the sea and sky. Try to keep other beachgoers at the edges of the frame, or wait for a gap.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the loungers to lock focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly to keep the sand from turning white. Take a Live Photo too, as the moving water can give you a nicer frame to choose from.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon toward sunset, when the golden light is strongest. For fewer people in the frame, go early in the morning.

text.access_note: The beach is public, but the pink loungers and beach club area belong to the hotel, so check the official site and current access rules before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The beach can be crowded, so early morning may mean fewer people in the frame.
Late afternoon toward sunset gives the strongest golden light at the beach.

name: Fairmont Royal Pavilion
label: Royal Pavilion
camera_source: Commons cluster (1 photos), weak. Moved 75 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 75 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/726763988: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fairmont Royal Pavilion Resort' (334 m across).
notes: Pink beachfront luxury resort on the Platinum Coast.

text.description:
The Fairmont Royal Pavilion is a beachfront hotel on Barbados's west coast, set in about 11 acres of gardens. It began life in the 1940s as the Miramar Hotel, the first hotel built on this coast, with just 12 rooms. That original building is now home to the Palm Terrace Restaurant. The Miramar was bought by a private investor in April 1987, restored, and reopened in December 1987. It has since grown into a hotel and private residence estate.

The resort is a large site, so it suits a wide, relaxed view better than one tight shot. Low buildings, planted gardens and open sky make an easy, colourful scene for a phone. Because the grounds are so spread out, step back far enough to fit the main buildings and some greenery together, rather than aiming at one doorway.

Face that way and take a general view first, then move in for details such as planting, a terrace or the building's lines. Keep to the public side of the property and respect the privacy of guests. Take a few frames in both portrait and landscape orientation, because the grounds look quite different in each.
text.geographic_location: On the west coast of Barbados, in the Holetown area of St. James, on the beach side and about half a mile from the nearest shopping centre in Holetown.
text.directions_text: The resort lies about half a mile from the shopping centre in Holetown. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the buildings and gardens. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want more of the grounds in the frame. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for architectural details or planting.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (on the sand directly in front of the Fairmont Royal Pavilion, looking back at the hotel). The resort's beachfront with palms and turquoise water in the foreground, framed by the hotel's gardens. Keep to areas open to the public and do not walk into guest areas.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the main building on one of the lower lines, leaving plenty of sky above. Include a little foreground greenery to give a sense of depth. Hold the phone level so the roof lines stay straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. If the shot feels flat, try portrait orientation as well as landscape.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday, and gentler shadows on the buildings.

text.access_note: The resort is a private hotel estate, so check the official site before you go to find out what is open to non-guests.
claims_not_in_sources: The sea lies to the west of the resort, as it is on Barbados's west coast.
Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer than midday light.
The area around the stand-here point is likely to be accessible to the public, while guest areas of the resort are private.

name: Folkestone Marine Park
label: Folkestone Park
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/5106250261: the OpenStreetMap point 'McGill Bellairs Research Institute'.
notes: Marine park and museum on the Holetown beachfront, with a snorkel trail and lifeguard station.

text.description: This stop covers the Folkestone Marine Park stretch of Holetown's coast and its neighbour, the Bellairs Research Institute, a marine biology field station on the Barbados west coast. It is a calm, low-key place to photograph: a working seaside research site with the Caribbean just beyond it, rather than a grand monument. The institute was founded in 1954 for McGill University, the Canadian university in Montreal, and was funded at first by a bequest from the British naval commander Carlyon Bellairs, who gave it his name. It sits between the Folkestone Marine Park and Museum to the south and the Coral Reef Club hotel to the north, so the buildings, trees and sea make a good local-scene shot. Just offshore is Folkestone Reef, made up of two flame-shaped formations that researchers call North and South Bellairs. The southern one reaches about 275 metres from shore and the northern one about 107 metres. Take a wide shot first to show the setting, then a closer one of the buildings and shoreline. Keep the horizon level using the gridlines, and be tactful about the people and activity around the site. The reef is under the water, so don't expect it to show clearly in a phone photo from the shore.
text.geographic_location: Just north of the historic town of Holetown, in the parish of St James on Barbados's west coast. It lies between the Folkestone Marine Park and Museum to the south and the Coral Reef Club hotel to the north.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop serves this spot, so start from Holetown town centre and head north along the coast by road, looking for Folkestone Marine Park. From it, the Bellairs Research Institute is about 80 metres to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 80 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the shoreline, sea and sky together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the institute's buildings. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details from 80 metres away.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 80 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line. Include some foreground such as grass, sand or a tree edge to give depth. Take one wide frame of the whole scene and one tighter frame of the buildings with the default lens (1x) or a little zoom.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sea or sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the bright water looks washed out. Try a Live Photo if there are waves or palms moving in the breeze.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light, and the sun would be behind you when facing north-east. Early morning is also a good time and is often quieter.

text.access_note: The institute is a working research facility, so photograph it from public areas and check the official site before you go for the park and museum access.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon sun would be behind a photographer at the stand-here point facing north-east, giving softer, warmer light.
Early morning is often quieter.
The reef will not show clearly in a phone photo taken from the shore.
The institute is a working site, so photographers should keep to public areas.
Holetown town centre is south of the spot, so heading north along the coast reaches it.

name: Chattel Village
label: Chattel Village
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Highway 1' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Highway 1 nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM N445314326 (Chattel Village): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Colourful chattel-house-style shopping and dining village.

text.description:
Chattel Village is a collection of brightly painted chattel houses in Holetown, and it is easy to photograph without going far out of your way. The houses are painted in pastel shades and have decorative fretwork and gable roofs. Tropical greenery and little paths run between them, which gives you plenty of colour and texture to work with.

The quickest picture is from the roadside on Highway 1. The village can be seen from the main road, with the houses set back a little and the roadside in the foreground. That gives you one wide frame of the whole group, and you don't need to go into the grounds for it. If you do want to go in, there are close-up shots to be had of fretwork, shutters, doors and the colours against the green. Shop opening hours and any rules about photography inside the grounds weren't confirmed, so check on arrival.

The roadside is next to a busy highway. Cross only at a designated pedestrian crossing and keep an eye on the traffic while you line up your shot. Keep your phone steady with both hands and take a few frames, in case a vehicle passes through the foreground. Then walk a little closer for the detail shots. Keep the camera level so the roof lines and walls stay straight.
text.geographic_location: Chattel Village is on the main road (Highway 1) through Holetown, south of the Holetown Monument. The roadside view is opposite the Sunset Crest Beach Club.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed here; walk from the Holetown Monument. From the monument, walk south along Highway 1 to the roadside opposite the Sunset Crest Beach Club. Confirm the exact standing point on the map, as guides differ slightly on which side of the road the village sits. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural wide view of the houses from the road. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for fretwork and gables. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close inside the grounds, as it will stretch the road and make the houses look smaller from the roadside.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Highway 1 (opposite the Sunset Crest Beach Club, on the roadside facing the village, reached by walking south from the Holetown Monument). The village's brightly painted houses seen set back from the main road, with the roadside in the foreground. From here the painted houses are to the south-east, set back from the road. The roadside is in the foreground of your shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the row of houses along the upper third, with the roadside and greenery below. Keep the phone level so the walls stay upright. If you go into the grounds, an alternative is to frame a single house with its fretwork and gable roof, using the paths and greenery as a frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a brightly painted wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the pastel colours don't wash out in strong sun. Take a few frames in a row, in case traffic passes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and richer colour than midday sun.

text.access_note: The roadside view from Highway 1 is open to anyone, but the village grounds and shops may have their own rules, so check on arrival.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer and gives richer colours than midday sun.
Strong sun can wash out pale pastel colours, so lowering the exposure slider slightly helps.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) tends to stretch the road and make the houses look smaller when used from the roadside.

name: Holetown Monument
label: Holetown Monument
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Holetown Monument' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM N6811499098 (Holetown monument): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Marks the 1627 landing of the first English settlers.

text.description:
Holetown Monument is a small white obelisk beside Highway 1 in the centre of Holetown. It commemorates the early landing at Holetown, and the plaque gives a date. Bronze settler figures and a flagpole stand with it, so there is more to see than the obelisk alone. It is a short, free stop, and it is the sight most visitors look for in the town.

It photographs well because the pieces sit together. From the front you can fit the obelisk, its commemorative plaque, the settler figures and the flag into one frame. The white stone is easy to pick out, which gives a clean, simple picture.

One detail to know if you caption your photo: the plaque reads 1605, while most accounts give 1625 for the landing. Check the date before you write a caption.

Stand on the roadside, on the side facing Highway 1, where the plaque and obelisk are both visible. Expect passing traffic, so keep your back to the kerb and watch your step. A few minutes is enough. If cars cross your frame, wait a moment and take the shot in the next gap.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Holetown, Barbados, right beside Highway 1. It is on the roadside in the middle of the town, so it is easy to find on foot.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops serve this spot. Head for the centre of Holetown and look for the white obelisk beside Highway 1. If you are coming from further away, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Holetown Monument. Once you are in the centre of town, the monument is only a short stroll along the roadside. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the obelisk, plaque and figures together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you cannot step back far enough, and keep the obelisk in the middle of the frame so its sides do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. At Holetown Monument, on the roadside facing Highway 1. From here the plaque and obelisk face you, with the bronze settler figures and flagpole in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the obelisk up with a vertical line so it stands straight. Frame it from the front, with the plaque and the settler figures low in the picture and the flag beside them. Then take a closer second shot of the plaque with the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) so the wording is easy to read.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white obelisk to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the stone keeps its detail and does not turn into a plain white shape.

text.access_note: It is an open roadside monument in the town centre; no entry is needed, but take care of the traffic on Highway 1.
claims_not_in_sources: A white stone obelisk may lose detail in bright light, so lowering the exposure helps.
Stepping back may be limited by the roadside and traffic, which is why the ultra-wide (0.5x) is suggested as an option.
Traffic on Highway 1 passes in gaps, so waiting a moment can clear the frame.
No station, tram or rail stops serve the spot, so a taxi or hired scooter is the suggested way to reach it.

name: St. James Parish Church
label: St. James Church
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/384916728: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. James Parish Church' (37 m across).
notes: Historic Anglican church, among the oldest in Barbados, on the site of the first English settlement.

text.description:
St. James Parish Church is a historic church just north of Holetown, and it sits on land that Barbadians often call "God's acre", one of the oldest consecrated plots on the island. The first settlers landed at Holetown in February 1627, and a wooden church was built here in 1628. A stone building made of local coral and limestone replaced it in the early 1690s. In 1874 the walls were rebuilt larger and the nave roof was raised on new pillars and arches. The enlarged church was consecrated by Bishop Mitchinson on Easter Tuesday, 1875, and most of what you see today dates from then. The sanctuary and north porch were added in the 1900s.

For a phone photo, the appeal is the old stone building set among gravestones and trees, with the churchyard giving you a natural foreground. Look for a clear gap between trees and parked cars, and keep the walls straight by lining them up with the gridlines.

If you go in, two details are worth a close-up: the old bell, said to be the oldest in Barbados and inscribed 1696, and the font in the baptistery, which bears the date 1684. Outside, the walled Alleyne family burial plot is in the north-east corner of the grounds.
text.geographic_location: The church is just north of the centre of Holetown, in the parish of St. James, beside Folkestone Park.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Holetown and head north towards the church, which is beside Folkestone Park. There are no rail or tram stops here, so come on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole church. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if trees or the boundary force you too close, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the porch, the tower and gravestone details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the church walls with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Include a few gravestones or a patch of grass in the lower part of the frame to give depth. For a tighter picture, zoom in on the tower and porch instead of walking closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sunlit stone to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale walls do not turn white. Portrait mode works well for a person standing among the gravestones, and Live Photos can catch passing movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and warmer colour on the stone, and fewer people in the grounds.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship with a churchyard, so dress modestly, be quiet during services, and check the official site or the parish before you go for visiting times and any rules on photography inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer and warmer on stone buildings.
There may be trees, parked cars or a boundary between the stand-here point and the church that affect the view.
Visiting times and photography rules inside a church can vary, and it is a good idea to dress modestly and be quiet during services.
